query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dynamic response of as‐cast, Co–free FeNiCrMn is governed by the balance between temperature‐dependent dislocation nucleation and dynamic recovery, such that at lower temperatures and higher strain rates limited recovery leads to rapid dislocation accumulation, enhanced strain hardening, and serrated flow, while at higher temperatures increased dislocation mobility promotes dynamic recovery resulting in smoother, lower yield stress deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast, solidified Co–free FeNiCrMn alloy with a homogeneous microstructure and minimal secondary phases
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to uniaxial tension and compression tests across a matrix of temperatures (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 600 K, 900 K) and strain rates (ranging from quasi‐static ~10^–3 s^–1 to high dynamic rates ~10^3 s^–1)
generation.conditions: Controlled laboratory testing with precise temperature control and strain rate monitoring, ensuring minimal compositional and defect state variations
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of the dislocation structure—including dislocation nucleation, pile‐up, and dynamic recovery (dislocation annihilation and rearrangement) events that may lead to serrated flow or smooth plastic deformation
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures and high strain rates, limited thermally activated recovery results in rapid dislocation accumulation and intermittent slip (serrations), whereas at high temperatures enhanced dislocation mobility facilitates dynamic recovery, lowering yield stress and producing smoother stress–strain curves
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in strain rate at low temperatures will yield higher yield strengths and a serrated stress–strain response due to rapid dislocation accumulation; conversely, at higher temperatures, the alloy will exhibit lower yield strengths and smoother flow as dynamic recovery mitigates dislocation build-up
generation.baseline: Room temperature (approximately 300 K) at moderate strain rates serves as the reference condition for comparing yield strength and flow stress behavior
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to as‐cast Co–free FeNiCrMn alloys with a uniform microstructure; deviations might occur if significant phase separation, precipitation, or other non‐dislocation-based mechanisms dominate the deformation response
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of dislocation nucleation versus recovery and the exact temperature–strain rate transition points require further calibration, and minor compositional inhomogeneities could also affect the observed dynamic behavior

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of homogeneous, as-cast Co–free FeNiCrMn samples. Subject each sample to a series of uniaxial tensile and compression tests under tightly controlled environments spanning temperatures of 77 K, 300 K, 600 K, and 900 K, and strain rates from 10^–3 s^–1 to 10^3 s^–1. In-situ high-speed imaging and post-test microscopic analyses (e.g., electron microscopy) should be employed to correlate dislocation structures with macroscopic stress–strain responses.
measurements: Yield strength and flow stress curves
Presence and magnitude of stress serrations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if (a) no significant differences in yield strength or serration behavior are observed across the temperature and strain-rate range (i.e., the stress–strain curves remain unchanged), or (b) if microstructural analyses do not reveal a systematic correlation between dislocation structures (and dynamic recovery phenomena) and the observed macroscopic mechanical behavior.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are new alloys that contain five or more elements in roughly-equal proportion. We present new experiments and theory on the deformation behavior of HEAs under slow stretching (straining), and observe differences, compared to conventional alloys with fewer elements. For a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates, HEAs deform in a jerky way, with sudden slips that make it difficult to precisely control the deformation. An analytic model explains these slips as avalanches of slipping weak spots and predicts the observed slip statistics, stress-strain curves, and their dependence on temperature, strain-rate, and material composition. The ratio of the weak spots’ healing rate to the strain-rate is the main tuning parameter, reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier effect and time-temperature superposition in polymers. Our model predictions agree with the experimental results. The proposed widely-applicable deformation mechanism is useful for deformation control and alloy design.
